holdings.name: Amazon.com Inc.
holdings.thesis:
I have started buying Amazon at $97.25 due to the recent bear market, where the company's stock dropped significantly. The whole technology market saw a decrease due to the sell-off of growth stocks that were overvalued, but I think that the market overlooks Amazon's significant presence in the cloud space and its most profitable segment, AWS. The company's retail segment was growing rapidly before pandemic restrictions, but the growth was artificial and caused by panic buying and people having more leisure time to buy non-necessity goods. After the pandemic, Amazon had to close the warehouses it opened to meet demand, so I believe that now the retail segment will stop growing rapidly, not because of negative trends but because the company deliberately reduces its footprint in it.

This conclusion is based on calculations: the shares are priced at 1.9 times sales, and the company's value is about $992 billion, which is a relatively low price for such a giant, despite a significant one-time write-down of the investment in Rivian and heavy R&D spending. Sales growth is close to 10% despite overall decline in consumer spending, and the operating income is positive despite one-time expenses, which suggests that the company has an excellent income-generating base that delivers a stable profit. Its value is about 18.6 times EBITDA, which is also a fair price. The last statistic that attracted me was the company's debt: $54.3 billion in cash against $67.2 billion, which is not a high number given the scale of Amazon's operations. I believe that the discrepancy between the high value of the company and the income from operations is what will bring good returns in the future.

My initial investment in the company is justified by the fact that AWS dominates the cloud computing market and is expected to grow in the future due to its adoption by various organizations. Advertising, which I did not consider before investing, also became a profitable segment for the company. Finally, the profit from retail sales increased more rapidly than I expected due to significant warehouse closures and optimization of costs. Now, instead of a loss, the company has a stable profit margin across all segments of its work.

In the future, I will monitor the expenditures on cloud technologies, including artificial intelligence, to ensure that they are not too high in the short term because such a move might eliminate the possibility of profit growth in the near future. Thus, Amazon is my favorite stock to invest in the long term, and I do not plan to sell it in the near future.

holdings.name: Bank Of America Corp.
holdings.thesis:
I am buying Bank of America at $41.96 because I think it is set up to earn more over the next few years. The Federal Reserve just cut interest rates in September 2024. Lower rates should help a bank like BofA, because it pays less on deposits while its loans keep earning more, which should increase its net interest income. I also expect deal activity to pick up, which helps its investment banking business.

I like that BofA is not just one business. It has a huge retail bank with the biggest and stickiest deposit base of any major U.S. bank, plus investment banking and wealth management. That makes it one of the most important banks in the country, and I think the mix is safer than a bank that depends on only one thing.

I am buying at about 13 times earnings for a bank with a return on equity above 9 percent. That looks cheap for a bank of this quality, and I think its returns can improve as net interest income and deal activity grow.

---UPDATE---

I continue to hold this because the interest income has grown as I had expected, and Bank of America has been quietly buying back a tremendous amount of its stock, growing my share of the company without me having to do a thing. The deposit base that convinced me to buy has held up through more than one round of bank-sector stress since then.

I do not expect this stock to have much of a move, and that's the whole point. It is meant to grow steadily in the background, supported by a size advantage that smaller banks cannot begin to match, and I plan to hold it as a long-term core position instead of trading around every rate headline.

holdings.name: Citigroup Inc
holdings.thesis:
I am buying Citi stock at $50.36 as a value and turnaround play. The stock trades at a significant discount to its tangible book value, and offers the best value among the big US banks in my opinion. Years of difficult and dysfunctional international diversification and large expenses have taken their toll. The new CEO Jane Fraser has started a turnaround plan, selling off non-core businesses and focusing on cutting costs across the board, and I want to buy now ahead of this new "era."

The numbers support this view. At 0.59 times tangible book value, the stock is trading below what the bank believes its business is worth. With 1.9 billion shares outstanding, the company is worth about $95.7 billion at the current price. At 12.5x earnings and a mid-single-digit return on equity, there appears to be limited downside based on its current value. At the same time, there is room for profitability and cost-cutting to improve, which could give the stock significant upside if the strategy works.

I believe my decision to buy the stock is supported by both its value and its long-term potential. The turnaround is making progress, as Citi continues to reduce its exposure to non-core international retail banking, cut costs, and improve profitability. The stock also remains attractively valued compared to its peers, even though it has risen since I first bought it. The large discount to tangible book value that originally attracted me is still there, although it has become smaller.

I am investing based on a long-term view and am willing to wait while the bank continues its restructuring and cost-cutting efforts over the next few years. Turnarounds are rarely smooth, so I'm aware the stock will likely remain somewhat volatile as Citi works to improve earnings and control costs. However, I believe the company's fundamentals can continue to improve over time.

holdings.name: Cadence Design Systems, Inc.
holdings.thesis:
I am buying Cadence Design Systems for $174.40. It is not a household name outside the chip industry, but it is one of only two major companies that make the design software that chip companies need to design modern semiconductors. That gives me exposure to the growth of the chip industry without the risks of owning an actual chipmaker, since these companies need Cadence's tools regardless of where they are in their product cycle.

The numbers also support the price I am paying. At around 53 times earnings and 13 times sales, the stock is expensive by most measures, but gross margins near 89 percent and operating margins around 28 percent show that this business operates more like a top-tier software company. Revenue is growing around 18 percent a year, and the company has almost no debt, with about $0.65 billion in debt compared to $0.79 billion in cash. This makes the valuation more reasonable for a business that does not need much money to keep growing.

I still hold this stock and am happy to do so, since the AI boom has turned out to be an even bigger boost to the business than I expected when I bought it. Every new AI chip, from custom chips to more complex designs, needs to go through software like this, and the growing complexity of chip design has only made these tools more important. It is a high-margin business with recurring revenue and a long-term growth trend as chip designs become more complicated. I see no reason to sell early.

The main thing I am watching going forward is the price, since this stock has never been cheap, but I think the quality of the business has made the valuation worth it.

holdings.name: GE Aerospace
holdings.thesis:
I am buying GE at $105.40 while the company splits into three separate businesses: GE Aerospace, GE Vernova, and GE HealthCare. What I really want is the aerospace side, GE Aerospace, since jet engines make most of their money years after they're sold, through decades of repairs, maintenance, and spare parts and not the original sale.

I believe splitting this business from the rest of the old industrial company, which has struggled for years with underperforming divisions and heavy pension costs, will help management to focus and actually run it effectively. The numbers I have access to are messy because of the split, but they still support my idea. The aerospace business is growing revenue more than 20 percent a year, with operating margins of around 20 percent, helped by more people flying again and a growing number of engines out there needing service. GE has more cash than debt heading into the split, about $17.3 billion in cash against $18.4 billion in debt at the company level, so the new standalone business will not start out buried in debt like some past GE restructurings.

---UPDATE---

I have held on to GE Aerospace because the plan worked out how I hoped, a more focused management team, a cleaner balance sheet, and a business that is benefiting directly from more people flying around the world. The distraction of running an unrelated healthcare and power business along with aerospace is gone. GE Vernova, the energy business, has done better since the split, but I wanted to limit my energy exposure and I wanted the aerospace side, which is still why I own it.

With so many engines already in use that need years of maintenance work, including the LEAP engine (the newer engine for the Boeing 737 MAX and Airbus A320neo), the steady repair-and-parts income I was counting on when I bought is now showing up clearly in the segment's own numbers instead of being buried inside a bigger company. I don't see much reason to sell this one early and think it's a position I want to hold long-term barring any major developments in the sector.

metricsAtPurchase.asOf: ~late 2023 / early 2024, pre-Vernova spinoff (FY2023 results, Aerospace segment)

holdings.name: Lilly (Eli) & Co
holdings.thesis:
I am buying Eli Lilly at $359.17 betting on the company's drugs to extend significantly beyond diabetes into the weight loss space, where they are currently in trials. The value of the data supporting tirzepatide, sold as Mounjaro for the treatment of diabetes, is better than the competition, and I think the company is in a good spot to create one of the largest pharmaceutical franchises in the industry if obesity therapy and insurance coverage take place in the way I hope for the next several years.

I understand that I am paying a premium. Shares were trading at around 52 times earnings and over 11 times sales, a price that only makes sense if the growth idea really takes off and not based on what the company earns now. What makes me feel confident enough to pay this price is a return on equity near 50 percent and gross margins over 75 percent, indicators that this was already a very well-run, efficient business before the opportunity in weight loss really took off, supported by a market cap nearly $323 billion and fairly manageable debt of $18.7 billion.

---UPDATE---

I still hold this, and it is one of my best performing positions in the entire portfolio. Mounjaro and its weight-loss version Zepbound have exceeded my initial expectations, insurance coverage has grown faster than I anticipated and Lilly's pipeline of drugs behind these products tells me this is not a one-drug story and rather a shift in production and what the company can do.

Valuation is my primary concern ahead, since a lot of future growth is already wrapped up in the stock price, but given how massive the market for obesity and metabolic disease treatment could be worldwide, I am comfortable holding on through the ups and downs rather than trying to time an exit around any one data release or competitor announcement.

holdings.name: NextEra Energy Inc
holdings.thesis:
I'm buying NextEra Energy at $78.69 to diversify my portfolio into a reliable income-producing asset that has less volatility than some of my other higher-growth stocks. NextEra is the largest utility company by market value and, to a lesser extent, the largest wind and solar power producer in the world. So I'm getting the dual benefit of a stable regulated utility with a generous dividend, and an economic moat in the renewable energy sector, which I think will see significant growth in the decades to come.

NextEra's financials support the fair valuation, as a utility with a P/E ratio of around 27 on adjusted earnings is still quite expensive. But an 11% return on equity and consistently high-teens operating margins are befitting of a power producer with a large installed base of electricity generation and distribution infrastructure to tap into. The balance sheet is levered, with around $74.4 billion in debt against under $1 billion in cash, which is entirely reasonable for a capital-intensive utility that requires constant investment in power generation facilities and electric grid infrastructure to continue its operations. The cash flow from operations is sufficient to fund the capital expenditures required to maintain the growth trajectory.

I'm buying NextEra Energy because it does exactly what I want as an investor: it provides reliable but unexciting returns through steady growth without having to think about it too much. The next generation of renewables is providing a nice tailwind for the stock, as constructing wind and solar farms is a profitable field for NextEra to occupy in a regulated monopoly setting. The increase in electricity consumption from data centers and the transition to electric vehicles and heat pumps will become a tailwind for the utility that I'm quite excited about, and it was a factor I hadn't considered when I made the decision to buy the stock.

It will continue to be one of the highest-yielding and most dependable stocks in my portfolio in years to come.

holdings.name: NVIDIA Corp
holdings.thesis:
I am buying NVIDIA at $17.55, in anticipation of the market realizing how AI infrastructure is one of the biggest investment trends for the next several years to decade. NVIDIA is the source of most chips used in training AI models, with their CUDA software forming the foundation of current machine learning research, making it incredibly difficult to move away from despite competition in the chip space.

The price is not cheap, as I'm buying it at around 100x earnings, but I believe that in a year when revenue is flat and earnings dropped by over 50% due to writedowns of inventory in the gaming graphics card segment due to lower demand after the pandemic (most likely explained by the decrease in working from home and leisure time), the fundamentals are still incredibly strong, with gross margins staying near 57% and return on equity of around 19% in the same period, showing that NVIDIA is a fundamentally strong company with growth potential that is currently being hampered by a temporary downturn in demand in one segment.

---UPDATE---

I have continued to hold on to this stock, and it has been the single strongest position in my portfolio, as the competitive advantage holds strong, being incredibly difficult to overcome despite the rise of other chipmakers with considerable funding backing them. Each step in the adoption of new AI methods and technologies required more and more computing power, and NVIDIA has been able to retain its position as the primary supplier for both chips and software for each new generation of technology.

I have not sold any shares as the position grew in size as a large portion of my portfolio due to the overall rise of the position, as I believe that the overall trend has a long way to go before peaking, and I did not want to cap my gains on a stock that is very hard to bet against, since its strong business and network effects keep it ahead of the competition. I keep a close eye on potential competition and the risk of revenue concentration on a few large customers, but none of it has cooled my overall enthusiasm for the stock.

holdings.name: PayPal Holdings Inc
holdings.thesis:
I am buying PayPal at $79.17 on the belief that the market overreacted to the soft growth and increased competition. PayPal is one of the largest online payment processors with a strong brand name and wide merchant acceptance, and Venmo has significant monetization potential that the company has not yet fully realized given its size.

The price supports my thesis, as I am buying under four times sales and twenty times non-GAAP earnings for a company that is still growing its revenue at a high single-digit rate, generating meaningful free cash flow, and has a balance sheet worth over $10 billion in cash against about the same amount of debt. With around 1.14 billion shares outstanding and a market cap near $90.4 billion, this is not the sign of a value trap but rather a lack of interest from the market due to fears of competition.

---UPDATE---

I am still long the stock, although I must admit it has not gone the way I wanted, and it is currently under my entry cost. Competition in checkout, particularly with Apple Pay and buy-now-pay-later firms, has been more challenging than I expected, and maintaining branded checkout share has proven more difficult than I had anticipated.

What has kept me long is the shift in focus from volume to profitability and quality growth under new leadership, and the price looks more reasonable now given the risk-reward situation, as much of the competition concern is already priced in. I am watching this closely and will reevaluate if things do not continue to improve.

holdings.name: Restaurant Brands International Inc
holdings.thesis:
I am buying Restaurant Brands International at $66.67 for its combination of steady cash flow and a turnaround in the works at Burger King. As a company with three big brands, Burger King, Tim Hortons, and Popeyes, I am not putting all my eggs in one basket. Tim Hortons remains a dominant Canadian brand with loyal customers, Popeyes is growing its presence internationally, and Burger King's plan to renew its restaurants and update its kitchens gives me confidence that years of neglect will finally be overcome.

The numbers support a fair price. Traded at around 22 times adjusted earnings and 3 times sales with a market value of nearly $20.1 billion, Restaurant Brands International is not a steal, but operating margins in the mid-30s thanks to the franchise model and revenue growth of nearly 14 percent this year show a company that is making good money without much of its own investment. In addition to a nice dividend while waiting for the turnaround at Burger King to really take off in the sales numbers, I am getting a reliable cash flow from the company.

---UPDATE---

I am continuing to hold this investment because the turnaround has taken on a slow and steady pace rather than a spectacular leap that would exceed my expectations for a restaurant remodeling program. I am not looking for a fast-growing stock and do not expect one, but the cash flow supports the dividend and allows for continued reinvestment in the Burger King fix.

I think of this as a lower-risk, income-producing alternative to higher-growth peers in my portfolio, and am quite happy to hold out for slow progress in the turnaround process as long as the sales trends continue to move in the right direction.

holdings.name: Charles Schwab Corp.
holdings.thesis:
I am buying Charles Schwab at $94.94 due to the 2023 regional bank crisis, where concerns about banks' losses on their bond portfolios dragged down Schwab's price despite its fundamental difference from a typical banking institution. Schwab runs the largest brokerage and custodial platform in the country with tens of billions of dollars in client funds, and I believe that the current selloff is a temporary balance-sheet scare that hides the true value of Schwab's extremely loyal customer base that takes decades to build.

At the price I'm buying, the stock is at about 32.6 times earnings. That is a high price, and I think it means the market is looking past Schwab's current problems. People will pay a lot for today's earnings when they think earnings are low now but will be higher later. Net margins well above 30 percent and a mid-teens return on equity suggest that the company's core operations remained healthy throughout the period of turmoil; the stock price is simply catching up to that reality.

I also like that Schwab is a low-cost provider. It keeps investing in technology to win over individual investors who do not have an advisor. It also has a platform for advisors (called RIAs). Having both gives Schwab more than one way to win over time.

I expect to stay long given that is precisely the scenario that played out. The deposit pressures that caused the 2023 panic have eased off as expected once the panic subsided, and the combination with TD Ameritrade, which preceded my purchase, has continued to deliver cost savings and additional business from cross-selling to shared customers.

I believe the 2023 panic provided a better entry point than justified by the fundamentals, and Schwab's dominant position in the wealth management and custody space is difficult to overcome by smaller regional competitors. I expect the position to continue to benefit from the merger synergies being realized over the coming years.

metricsAtPurchase.asOf: ~2024, after the 2023 deposit-flight scare eased (FY2023 annual results)
metricsAtPurchase.note: Bought as the stock recovered off its March 2023 regional-bank-crisis low, not at the trough itself — the price better matches a 2024 entry.

holdings.name: Tesla Inc
holdings.thesis:
I am buying Tesla at $351.80 because I want exposure to the EV maker that has demonstrated the most significant cost advantage over its peers through years of vertical integration and innovation in production processes that have proven difficult to mimic. Additionally, I see significant value in the energy storage segment, where Tesla has been investing heavily in battery production for stationary storage with grid-scale applications underpriced by the market. I am buying Tesla at a size that will be the largest position in my portfolio due to its volatile price movements driven by varying expectations about the company's prospects.

The valuation seems to require a heavy emphasis on future performance to justify its lofty multiple. Currently, Tesla's shares trade at around 100 times GAAP earnings and more than 12 times sales, giving the company a market capitalization of almost $1.22 trillion, making it one of the most expensive car manufacturers in the history of the market. However, with margins in Tesla's core business of 18 percent gross and 9 percent operating, well above the industry averages for most automakers of barely double digits, the company has demonstrated its ability to produce products at a cost significantly lower than many competitors, giving it a genuine competitive advantage.

I am buying Tesla because its core business continues to demonstrate cost advantages over the rivals that have emerged in the market for electric vehicles, including traditional automakers and new entrants from China, and a separate business of battery storage for the stationary market has become a substantial source of revenue with excellent margins not accounted for in the overall value of the automaker.

I am buying Tesla because I am willing to accept the largest range of possible outcomes for this particular investment in my portfolio, with positive and negative surprises on both sides of the equation that may cause the price to move sharply higher or lower, and because I want to take advantage of the unique opportunity to participate in a company that has disruptive potential in the long run. Position size is the largest in my portfolio due to the volatility of the stock, and I review Tesla-specific position reviews more frequently than others due to rapidly changing dynamics in the competitive environment.

holdings.name: Vertex Pharmaceuticals, Inc.
holdings.thesis:
I'm buying Vertex Pharmaceuticals at $369.50 because it has a virtual monopoly on the treatment for cystic fibrosis. There is no competitive product which acts on the underlying genetics rather than the symptoms, which provides Vertex with significant pricing power and a long runway before patents begin to expire and hurt the business. I want exposure to biotech without the potentially fatal risk of relying on a pipeline that has not yet delivered its goods, because while the main drug is approved and doing well, there is not that much risk involved.

Profits are unusually large for a biotech, with Vertex enjoying a 37 percent net margin and a 91 percent gross margin, figures that are typically only seen in drug companies that do not spend the money on research and development that Vertex spends, with an investment of approximately $10.7 billion in combined cash and investments and almost no debt. At about 29 times earnings for that level of quality, funded by a drug with basically no real competition, and a market cap near $97.5 billion, the fair price estimate given the typical profit rates for comparable growth is about right, with Vertex's cash flow allowing it to fund research into other diseases like non-opioid pain treatment and Type 1 diabetes without needing to turn to external funding or dilution to continue its research into mid-stage trials.

I'm buying this as it provides the security of a profitable core business that typically pays large amounts of cash like a royalty on the treatment for cystic fibrosis, while also providing the upside potential of a drug that can come out of its pipeline. It's one of the most balanced positions among the higher growth stocks in my portfolio.

holdings.name: ExxonMobil Holdings Corp.
holdings.thesis:
I am buying ExxonMobil at $118.05 on the belief that they've become far more conservative in spending. Following years of heavy spending on growth projects that the market punished the stock for, Exxon has evidently changed their approach to spending, directing growth capital towards their cheapest oil to produce, particularly the Permian Basin in Texas and offshore Guyana, as opposed to the lower-yielding projects it spent on during the last oil cycle.

The price reflects the market's belief that this won't last. I'm paying less than 9x earnings and approximately 9x free cash flow, with a market cap near $497 billion, for a company which just grew earnings more than 150 percent year-over-year fueled by high energy prices. Despite the stock's substantial rebound from its lows, the market is still pricing Exxon as if the stronger results and judicious spending won't be sustained, allowing me a healthy cushion, bolstered further by $29.6 billion in cash against $41.3 billion in debt.

---UPDATE---

I still hold this because Guyana has grown far faster and more profitably than I anticipated upon purchase, with each new phase coming online roughly on schedule, while management has maintained the judicious spending I was expecting as opposed to reverting to the spend-at-any-cost approach of the last oil cycle under previous leadership. The dividend and stock buybacks together provide me a tangible cash return as a shareholder while Guyana's next phases ramp up, and I view the refining and chemicals side of the business as a useful partial hedge against the volatility of oil prices that a pure oil-drilling company would not offer.

The bump several months ago from the US intervention also provided a nice boost to the stock, which I believe will continue.
